title: Read the Feed Like a Contract
scenario: It is 6:18 AM. The overnight price rows landed on schedule. Before anyone cleans or computes, inspect the feed the way a pipeline engineer would: what does each column promise, what quirks does today's file reveal, and who depends on it next?
input:
hub, peak, settled
ercot, $187/MWh, $142/MWh
SPP, $96/MWh, $88/MWh
miso, $74 /MWh, $70/MWh

Delivery: dropped nightly by the market data export, expected before 6:15 AM.
instructions: Read the header row, then read each data row slowly - the quirks are the lesson.
Validate to record the feed profile.

questions.prompt: What structure does this input have?

options.text: CSV rows under a header that names the columns
Free-form prose like the analyst note

questions.explain: The first line (hub, peak, settled) is a header naming the columns; every following line is one row honoring that order. That header is the feed's contract.

questions.prompt: Which quirks in today's file show the feed does NOT promise clean values?

options.text: The rows arrive in alphabetical order
Inconsistent hub casing (ercot, SPP, miso) and a stray space in "$74 /MWh"

questions.explain: Compare the hub values and the MISO peak cell character by character. Casing drifts and spacing drifts - the contract covers columns, not cleanliness.

questions.prompt: In a real company, what would consuming this feed require?

options.text: A market data subscription or permission to the nightly export location
Nothing - price data is always free

questions.explain: The input names its delivery: a nightly market data export. Reading it programmatically means access to that feed or drop location - a subscription and a permission, not a person.

questions.prompt: Which workflow step consumes these rows first?
questions.explain: Follow the map: raw rows cannot be computed on ($ signs, units, drift), so their first stop is the cleaning step that normalizes them.

artifactOnPass.knownQuirks: inconsistent hub casing; stray spaces; values carry $ and /MWh
artifactOnPass.accessNeeded: market data subscription or export-location permission

copilotPrompt: Profile this CSV feed as a contract: structure, columns, schedule, the quirks today's file reveals, the access consuming it requires, and its first consumer.
successMessage: Feed profiled. You already know exactly what the cleaning step will have to fix - because you found the quirks yourself.

intro.heading: Before you inspect: feeds are promises

sections.title: A header row is a contract
sections.body: hub, peak, settled is not just a label line - it is the producer's promise about every future file: these columns, this order. Pipelines are built against that promise.

sections.title: Contracts have gaps
sections.body: The contract says which columns arrive. It says nothing about casing, spacing, or units - and today's file drifts on all three. Reading one real file closely tells you what the contract does NOT cover.

sections.title: Schedule is part of the source
sections.body: This feed drops nightly before 6:15 AM. Schedules matter because everything downstream inherits them: a late feed is a late brief.

sections.title: Same rows, the Clean Price Data step
sections.body: These are the exact rows the Clean Price Data step normalizes. Inspection and transformation are two different skills applied to one input - first understand it, then fix it.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd download the overnight price file (a CSV or an emailed attachment) and load its rows into a table the workflow can read.

bestFit.how: 'When a file is created' on the feed folder, then Excel 'List rows in a table'
a Cron trigger plus a Read Binary File node when the vendor drops on a schedule

takeaway.heading: Feed profiled
points: You read the header as a contract and today's rows as evidence of what the contract leaves out.
You found the quirks by eye - casing drift, a stray space, units on every value - before any code had to.
You recorded the schedule and the access requirement, the two facts integration work always starts from.
Clean Price Data consumes exactly these rows; you now know why that step exists.
The workflow can now identify the raw numeric feed that must be cleaned before evaluation.
